Nonmonotone Backtracking

Source: R/line_search.R
nonmonotone.Rd

Performs Armijo backtracking that compares the trial value with the largest of the last few objective values and not with the current one, so a step may increase the objective.

Usage

nonmonotone(
  c1 = 1e-04,
  shrink = 0.5,
  memory = 10,
  max_step = 30,
  resolution = 0
)

Arguments

c1

Sufficient-decrease constant. Defaults to 1e-4.

shrink

Factor applied to the step on each backtrack. Defaults to 0.5.

memory

The number of earlier values, besides the current one, over which the reference is taken. Defaults to 10; 0 makes the search identical to armijo().

max_step

Maximum number of trial points, including the full step, before the search returns without a step. Defaults to 30.

resolution

The smallest difference in the objective that the objective can resolve, in the units of the objective, or a function of no arguments that returns it when it changes during the run. Defaults to 0, which disables the test; see armijo() for the purpose of the test and for the reason why it is applied at the full step, before the search begins.

Value

A line_search() object.

Details

The condition is that of Grippo, Lampariello and Lucidi: $$f(x_k + \alpha d_k) \le \max_{0 \le j \le m} f(x_{k-j}) + c_1 \alpha\, g_k^\top d_k,$$ which is Armijo's condition with the reference replaced by the largest of the last \(m+1\) values. An accepted step improves on the largest of the recent values, but it need not improve on the current one.

Purpose

Some methods are efficient because of steps that increase the objective. bb() is the main case: its step length is a curvature estimate taken from the last secant pair, and following that estimate sometimes leads to a higher value. An Armijo condition rejects every step that increases the objective and backtracks until it finds a shorter one, which removes the steps on which the method relies. On the Rosenbrock function bb() needs fewer than half as many evaluations of the objective under nonmonotone() as under armijo() (see the examples).

The cost is a weaker guarantee. A monotone method cannot cycle, since the objective is a decreasing sequence bounded below; a nonmonotone method relies on the finite memory for that, and its convergence result is more delicate. The search is intended for methods such as bb(), whose steps are not required to decrease the objective.

memory = 0

At memory = 0 the reference is the current value and the condition is exactly Armijo's, so nonmonotone(memory = 0) and armijo() produce the same run, and a comparison between the two settings isolates the effect of the memory.

No nonmonotone Wolfe search

The curvature condition concerns the gradient at the trial point and does not involve the value against which the decrease is measured. A nonmonotone Wolfe search would therefore be a fourth object and not an option of this one, and the package does not provide one.

References

Grippo, L., Lampariello, F. and Lucidi, S. (1986). A nonmonotone line search technique for Newton's method. SIAM Journal on Numerical Analysis 23, 707–716.

Raydan, M. (1997). The Barzilai and Borwein gradient method for the large scale unconstrained minimization problem. SIAM Journal on Optimization 7, 26–33.

See also

armijo() for the monotone version, bb() for the method that uses this one by default, line_search() for the parent class.

Examples

nonmonotone()
#> <line_search> nonmonotone backtracking (memory = 10)
nonmonotone(memory = 5)
#> <line_search> nonmonotone backtracking (memory = 5)

# The example shows the effect on bb(), the method that uses this search
# by default.
f  <- function(p) 100 * (p[2] - p[1]^2)^2 + (1 - p[1])^2
gr <- function(p) c(-400 * p[1] * (p[2] - p[1]^2) - 2 * (1 - p[1]),
                    200 * (p[2] - p[1]^2))
evals <- function(ls) minimize(bb(line_search = ls), f, c(-1.2, 1),
                               gr = gr)@counts[["f"]]
c(nonmonotone = evals(nonmonotone()), armijo = evals(armijo()))
#> nonmonotone      armijo 
#>          67         154 

# With memory = 0 the search is armijo(), so the comparison above
# isolates the memory.
identical(evals(nonmonotone(memory = 0)), evals(armijo()))
#> [1] TRUE
